handbookNote: Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP) Boating Division and its 2026 Connecticut Boater's Guide (portal.ct.gov/DEEP/Boating/Boating-and-Paddling) -- Connecticut has no single official state-administered boating knowledge exam that every boater must take; instead, Connecticut law requires any owner of a vessel required to be registered/numbered in the state, plus operators who are Connecticut residents or own real property in the state, to hold a valid boating certificate (a Safe Boating Certificate, a Certificate of Personal Watercraft Operation, or a qualifying U.S. Coast Guard license) before operating a motorboat or a sail-only sailboat 19.5 feet or longer, with narrow exceptions (e.g. a 106-lbs.-thrust-or-less electric motor on inland waters within a daylight window). Unlike many states, Connecticut's mandate is not keyed to a birth-date cutoff -- it is tied to vessel registration and the operator's residency/property ownership, with separate tiered age restrictions layered on top for younger operators (10-hp limit under 12, supervised operation under 16, PWC supervision rules, etc.). This mandate was independently confirmed by two sources: CT DEEP's own official boating certificate pages (portal.ct.gov/deep/boating/certification) and 2026 Boater's Guide PDF, cross-checked against the BoatUS Foundation's Connecticut course page, which independently states its own course is 'NOT Approved by Connecticut to satisfy the mandatory education requirements for boaters and PWC operators' -- confirming the mandate is real, not an Arizona-style false positive. Most boaters satisfy the requirement via one of nine DEEP-approved private/nonprofit course providers (America's Boating Club/US Power Squadrons, USCG Auxiliary, and several small private CT-specific providers -- notably NOT the large national online marketplaces like Boat-Ed or BOATERexam, which as of this build state on their own Connecticut pages that they cannot currently issue a CT card), each running an 8-hour combination basic-boating/PWC course (or an 8-hour basic course plus a separate 2.5-hour PWC upgrade course) ending in a proctored, DEEP-graded exam; because Connecticut's approved-course landscape is fragmented across small local/private providers rather than a big national vendor, no single publicly-published question-count/passing-score convergence exists across vendors the way it does in states that rely on Boat-Ed or BOATERexam, and that is honestly reported as unconfirmed rather than asserted. The one concretely confirmed official number is DEEP's own optional Equivalency Examination (an alternative to the 8-hour course, for experienced boaters only): a multiple-choice test with an 80%-or-higher passing score (78%-or-below failing), a $75 fee, offered only by DEEP in virtual or in-person sessions, and attemptable only once per person. Content is grounded in extensive real Connecticut-specific detail pulled directly from DEEP's own official 2026 Boater's Guide (36MB PDF, portal.ct.gov/-/media/deep/boating/boating_guide/ct-boaters-guide-english.pdf), including: the SBC/CPWO certificate framework and its reciprocity states (MA, NH, NY, RI) with a 90-day residency grace period; DMV vessel registration/titling (19.5-ft sail threshold, 2016 titling law for 2017-model-year-or-newer vessels at $25, HIN and decal placement rules, 6.35% vs. 2.99% sales/use tax cutover at July 1, 2018); required safety equipment tables by federal length class (A/1/2/3) covering fire extinguishers (12-year expiration rule effective April 20, 2022), ventilation, VDS (required only on coastal waters), sound-producing devices, backfire flame arrestors, and the post-January-1-2020 engine cut-off switch mandate (vessels under 26 ft, 115+ lbs. static thrust); PFD law including the under-13 always-wear rule, the October 1-May 31 universal wear rule for manually propelled vessels, and inflatable-PFD age/weight restrictions; Slow-No-Wake definition (<=6 mph) and its 100-foot (motorboats)/200-foot (PWC) near-shore distance rules; reckless operation and BUI (.08% general / .02% under-21, plus Connecticut's marijuana-intoxication DRE enforcement framework and its newly-enacted reciprocal BUI/DUI license-suspension law); PWC-specific rules (sunset-to-sunrise operating ban, no-passenger-in-front rule, shut-off lanyard, wake-jump restriction); Public Act 16-187's Jetted Articulated Vessel (flyboard) rules and the RCSA Section 15-121-A10 efoil/motorized-surfboard prohibition; the October 2015 Safe Water Skiing Endorsement law (100-ft towline cap, no elastic tow lines, 12-year-old-minimum observer, PWC-towing size/capacity minimums); accident reporting thresholds (>$500 property damage within 5 days; death/disappearance/injury-beyond-first-aid triggering immediate notification plus a 48-hour DEEP report) and the multi-agency enforcement structure (USCG, DEEP EnCon police, municipal police, town marine officers, lake patrolmen, POST-certified harbormasters) with warrantless stop-and-board authority; aids to navigation, movable-bridge signaling procedures, and the Thames River's federal Security Zones near the Electric Boat Shipyard (Groton), USCG Academy (New London), and Naval Submarine Base (Groton) -- plus universal NASBLA-aligned boating-safety fundamentals (Navigation Rules/right-of-way, hull types, cold-water immersion, trailering, and marine weather practices) applied to Connecticut's Long Island Sound coastal boating culture, including its tidal current 'gates' (The Race, Plum Gut) and seasonal nor'easter/hurricane exposure. Connecticut's Fire Marshal noise-limit fine schedule ($220/$435/$535) and the abandoned-boat process ($440 fine, 24-hour/45-day thresholds) are also drawn directly from the 2026 Boater's Guide -- price matches this project's Motorcycle-tier boating convention ($7.99), not a placeholder
